title: Assignment 1: graph & grid basics
overview: The first graded assignment. It checks that you can read a graph, look at adjacency lists directly, and run BFS on a grid to test reachability, count apartments (components) and measure their sizes. Each problem is a small twist on the Module 2-3 templates.

concepts.explain: To know whether `a → b` is one edge, scan `adj[a]` for `b`. No search needed.
Sorting `adj[x]` with `greater<int>()` gives neighbours in descending order.
Store the row/column of `A` and `B` as the grid is read, so BFS knows where to start and stop.
Loop over all cells; each unvisited floor cell starts a BFS and adds one apartment.
Start a counter at 1 and add 1 every time a new cell is pushed; return it from `bfs`.

files.title: Is there a direct edge A → B?
files.what: For each query it checks whether B appears in A's adjacency list (a node counts as connected to itself).
steps: `direct_edge(from, to)` returns true at once if `from == to`.
Print YES or NO for each query.
files.complexity: Time O(deg(A)) per query · Space O(V + E)
files.input_note: `n e`, e directed edges, `Q`, then Q lines `A B`.
files.output_note: Five answers, one per query: `0 1` YES (edge), `1 0` NO (wrong direction), `2 2` YES (same node), `0 3` NO (only through other nodes), `1 4` YES.
files.watch_out: With up to 10^6 edges and 10^6 queries, scanning a long list can be slow; an adjacency matrix (N <= 1000) gives O(1) answers.

check.q: Why does query `1 0` print NO when query `0 1` prints YES?
check.a: The graph is directed: only the arrow 0 → 1 exists.

files.title: Neighbours in descending order
files.what: For each query node X, sort its adjacency list in descending order and print it, or -1 if it has none.
steps: Store the undirected edges in both lists.
For query `x`, if `adj_list[x]` is empty print -1.
Else sort it with `greater<int>()` and print every value.
files.complexity: Time O(d log d) per query · Space O(V + E)
files.output_note: `-1` for node 3 (no edges), `4 1` for node 0, `2 0` for node 1.

check.q: What does the program print for a node with no edges?

files.title: Can we walk from room A to room B?
files.what: Finds the cells A and B while reading the map, then BFS from A through non-wall cells and stops when B is popped.
steps: While reading, remember `(Ai, Aj)` and `(Bi, Bj)`.
BFS from A; a neighbour is allowed if `valid`, unvisited and not `#`.
When the popped cell equals B, return true.
If the queue empties, return false. Print YES/NO.
files.input_note: `N M`, then the map with `.`, `#`, `A`, `B` (the sample from the statement).
files.output_note: Prints `YES`: A goes down the left corridor, along the bottom and up to B.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why does the BFS allow any cell that is not `#` instead of only `.`?
check.a: So it can also step onto the target cell `B` (and start from `A`).

files.title: Count apartments
files.what: Counts connected groups of `.` cells using BFS started from every unvisited floor cell.
steps: Double loop over cells; if a cell is `.` and not visited, `bfs(i, j)` and `count++`.
files.output_note: `3`: the two-cell room on the top left, the big room on the right, and the two-cell room on the bottom left.
files.watch_out: It uses global `vis` without `memset`; that is fine because global arrays start as all false.

check.q: Which earlier idea is this problem really?
check.a: Counting connected components, on a grid instead of an adjacency list.

files.title: Rooms in each apartment
files.what: Like problem 4, but `bfs` returns how many cells it visited; the sizes are sorted and printed (0 if none).
steps: `room_count` starts at 1 for the start cell.
Store every returned size in `apartments`, then sort ascending.
Print the sizes, or `0` if the vector is empty.
files.complexity: Time O(N·M + k log k) · Space O(N·M)
files.output_note: `2 2 8`: two small apartments with 2 rooms each, and one with 8.

check.a: The start cell is part of the apartment but is pushed before the counting loop.

recap: Read the question: a direct edge needs no BFS.
Record special cells (A, B, R, D) while reading the grid.
Grid component count = number of BFS/DFS starts.
Return the size from the search function to get component sizes.

check_yourself.q: How would problem 5 change to print the largest apartment only?
check_yourself.a: Keep a running `max` of the returned sizes instead of storing them all.

check_yourself.q: Global `bool vis[1005][1005]` is never cleared. Why is that safe here?
check_yourself.a: Globals are zero-initialised and the program runs only one search session.

body: This is the first graded assignment, so nothing on it is new. Every problem is one of the three tools from Modules 1 to 3 wearing a different hat. The hard part of an assignment day is not writing the code; it is reading a question and knowing within ten seconds which tool it is asking for.

Start with the question that needs no search at all. If someone asks "is there a road straight from A to B, with no other town in between?", you do not walk anywhere. You look at A's neighbour list and check whether B is written in it. BFS would give the right answer too, but it answers a much bigger question than the one asked, and on 10^6 queries that costs you the time limit.

Three of the five problems hand you a map instead of a list of edges, so it is worth saying once what a map and a graph have in common. A cell `(i, j)` **is** a node. Its neighbours are the four cells above, below, left and right of it.

The only difference is where the edges live. In a graph you stored them yourself in `adj_list`. In a grid nobody stores them, because you can work them out: add one of the four direction pairs to `(i, j)`, then let `valid(i, j)` tell you whether you have fallen off the map. So the BFS from Module 2 does not change at all. `visited` becomes two-dimensional, and "the neighbours of this node" becomes four additions.
Here is the pattern the grid problems share, on a map small enough to do by hand. `#` is a wall, `.` is floor, and you want the number of separate rooms.
intro.trace:
map            after the search from (0,1)
# . . #        #  1  1  #
# # . #        #  #  1  #
. . # #        .  .  #  #

next unvisited floor cell is (2,0)
               #  1  1  #
               #  #  1  #
               2  2  #  #

2 searches started  ->  2 apartments
sizes: 3 cells and 2 cells

body: You walked over the cells in reading order. The first floor cell you met that was not yet visited started a search, and that search swallowed the whole room, so every other cell of that room was already marked when the outer loop reached it. The number of searches you started is therefore the number of apartments, and if the search counts the cells it marks, that count is the size of one apartment. Those two lines of bookkeeping are problems 4 and 5.

**BFS or DFS?** For "can I get from A to B" and "how many rooms are there", both give the same answer, because both end up marking exactly the reachable cells. Choose BFS when the question mentions distance — fewest steps, shortest path, how many moves — because BFS finishes one level before starting the next, so the level on which a cell is found is its distance. Choose DFS when you only need to touch everything reachable and want shorter code, but remember that it recurses: on a 1000 x 1000 open map the recursion can go a million calls deep.

Two details catch people on this assignment. First, the special cells: `A` and `B` are not `.`, so a search that walks only on `.` will refuse to step onto its own target. Note their row and column while you are reading the map, and let the search walk on anything that is not a wall. Second, direction: in the first problem the edges are one-way, so `0 1` can be YES while `1 0` is NO. Push `b` into `adj_list[a]` and nothing back.
The five programs below are these ideas with the details filled in. Read each statement first, decide which of the three tools it wants, and only then look at the code.
